# Trust and security {#sec-trust-security}

[Normative]{.status}

Information is only useful if a receiver can decide how far to trust it.
This chapter defines how the origin and integrity of information can be verified,
who may publish and read what, and how the provenance of information is kept as it moves through the system.

## Authenticity

Every Thing can be authenticated with a **digital signature**. The framework distinguishes two kinds:

Ephemeral signatures
: Protect a communication session — for example TLS session keys.
  They show the information was not altered *in transit on that link*, but say nothing once it has arrived.

Persistent signatures
: Are attached to the information itself and stay with it when it is stored, relayed or re-published.
  They show who originated it, wherever it is found.

The two can be combined. Persistent signatures allow trust to be maintained as information journeys across several links and transports.

::: {.requirement #ncf-tru-001}
**NCF-TRU-001** · *Draft*\
It MUST be possible to attach a persistent signature to any Thing.
:::

The working proposal is to use JOSE: JWS [@rfc7515] for signatures and JWE [@rfc7516] for encryption,
applied to the JSON-LD representation, with identifiers for the algorithms used.
See [decision record 0004](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0004-trust-stack.md).

Some transports, such as AIS or NMEA 2000, may not have sufficient bandwidth to accommodate signatures or other message authentication tags.
The mechanism used to establish trust must be defined by each binding.

## Identity and authorization

The working proposal:

- **Servers** are identified by WebPKI certificates, which can be domain validated.
- **Data owners** are identified separately from servers, by certificates at one of two tiers (@sec-data-owners).
- **Clients** are identified using OpenID Connect [@oidc-core].
- **Authorization** uses OAuth 2.0 [@rfc6749], under policies set by the owner of each resource.

### Data owners {#sec-data-owners}

A data owner's certificate verifies its persistent signatures.
There are two tiers of confidence in a data owner's identity:

Tier 1: legal entity
: The data owner's identity as a legal entity is verified, in one of two ways:

  - **Trusted certificate authority.** A certificate authority on the framework's trust list verifies the data owner's identity and issues its certificate.
    Examples are a government certificate authority and an MCP identity registry [@iala-g1183].
    The certificate is independent of the data owner's servers.
  - **Validated domain.** The data owner publishes its certificate on its own domain, and the certificate names that domain.
    The server it is retrieved from has an organization-validated or extended-validation certificate, and the organization named in the data owner's certificate matches it.

Tier 2: internet presence
: Only the data owner's control of an internet identifier is verified, in one of two ways:

  - **Domain.** The data owner publishes its certificate on its own domain, and the certificate names that domain.
    The server it is retrieved from has a domain-validated certificate.
  - **Individual.** The data owner's certificate binds its key to its OpenID Connect identity [@oidc-core].
    For example, a certificate authority issues a short-lived certificate after the individual signs in, and records it in a transparency log [@sigstore-fulcio].
    The working assumption is that the identity comes from one of these OpenID Connect providers:
    providers of commonly used operating system platforms, such as Apple (iOS and macOS), Google (Android) and Microsoft (Windows);
    other well-known providers, such as social media or maritime providers;
    or providers with which the receiver has a private trust relationship, such as organizations, non-governmental organizations and manufacturers.

  Tier 2 suits data owners for whom tier 1 is impractical, such as individual operators, and scales to large numbers of them.

A receiver records which tier, and which way, applied when it verified a signature.

See [provisional decision 0014](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0014-data-owner-identity.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Who maintains the trust list for tier 1, and which certificate authorities does it include?
Is the list published with the framework, or maintained by participants, given that the framework operates no infrastructure (@sec-architecture)?
Root programs require hierarchies that issue TLS server certificates to be dedicated to TLS server authentication [@chrome-root-policy], so certificates from a trusted certificate authority come from other hierarchies.
Which verification of identity is required, for example that of the Extended Validation Guidelines [@cabf-evg]?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Verifying a certificate published on a domain depends on the domain still publishing it.
How is a signature verified after the key is replaced or the domain lapses: by publishing retired certificates, by receivers keeping evidence of retrieval, or by a transparency log?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How does a receiver decide which OpenID Connect providers it accepts for individuals?
Which participants or existing public services operate the certificate authority and transparency log for them?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How does a receiver learn that a data owner's certificate has been revoked?
Are signatures timestamped, so that they can be verified after the certificate expires?
How is the tier recorded in the provenance of a Thing?
:::

### Devices and responsible parties {#sec-responsible-parties}

A device's identity rolls up to one or more responsible parties: persons, organizations and vessels.
A device can have several responsible parties at once, each in a different role.
For example, data from a device on a chartered vessel can trace to:

- the vessel;
- the vessel's owners;
- the charter company;
- the charterer;
- the person in charge of the vessel, such as the master;
- a crew member.

Each link from a device to a responsible party is a relationship (@sec-relationships), so it can be signed, versioned and exchanged like any other Thing.

See [provisional decision 0016](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0016-responsible-parties.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Which roles of responsible parties need terms in the vocabularies?
Relationships change over time, for example with each charter: how is the period of a relationship recorded, so that a receiver can tell which responsible parties applied when data was produced?
Who may assert a relationship between a device and a responsible party, and does the responsible party have to confirm it?
Does a device sign data itself, or does a responsible party sign for it?
:::

Identity of vessels and on-board devices; role of official identifiers like MMSI alongside smaller vessels and mobile applications.
:::
